review_headline: Fantastically acted, a clever structure, but a few too many moments where the story runs out of steam
review_body:
Louisiana, 1995. A young girl's body is found tied to a tree, the victim of what appears to be a ritualistic murder. Two officers are assigned to the case: Martin Hart, a dyed-in-the-wool traditional detective who enjoys drinking and is having an affair, and Rust Cohle, a ferociously intelligent man who ponders philosophical and existentialist concepts whilst working. Over the course of seventeen years, the case is apparently solved but then re-opened again as Hart and Cohle, whose relationship suffers seismic shocks, face the possibility that they may have gotten things wrong.

True Detective is HBO's latest big-hitter series, an anthology show in which each season will be a different, self-contained story with its own locations and characters. This first season is set in Louisiana (after True Blood and Treme, HBO probably have a discount on filming there) and is focused on a very clever serial killer who knows how to make it look like he's disappeared whilst carrying on his work.

True Detective has won enormous plaudits for a number of its achievements, and I can only join the choir here. The cinematography is breathtaking, the sense of atmosphere and place vivid and the acting by everyone, but in particular Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey, is outstanding. The show's artistic ambition, using the traditional detective story framework to express thoughts and ideas about science, religion, nihilism, existentialism and corruption, is commendable. The structure of setting the story in three distinct timeframes and moving between them is also very successful, with the 1995 segment foreshadowing and the 2012 segment obliquely referencing things that happened in the 2002 segment which we then get to see unfold.

The show does have a number of problems, however. For a story that only lasts for eight hour-long episodes, the pacing often feels off. Some episodes are rammed full of incident, character development and thematic musings and are highly compelling. Others are almost bereft of substantial content until the obligatory end-of-episode cliffhanger. Or to put it another way, a show this short really shouldn't have such long periods which nothing much is going on. There is also the confusion of the show making frequent references to Robert W. Chambers's The King in Yellow (itself an inspiration for Lovecraft's Cthulu mythos) but then not making it clear that the book itself does not exist in the show's universe.

The series also hints that it may represent the end-point of what television as an art form can do, particularly on a short timescale. Rust Cohle returns to the ideas of the point of our existence in an empty universe, the struggling with the idea of an afterlife and the inescapable loneliness of being stuck inside our own skulls several times, but each time doesn't really develop them or have more to say on them. We get some great quotes out of these ruminations, but little more. This is because a TV show focused on a more traditional narrative drive simply hasn't got the time or space to delve into these ideas as well as a novel can. If this is the Golden Age of Television, True Detective hints at what might become its limiting factor.

Other complaints may be made, particularly over the thinness of the female characters and some rather completely out-of-place sex scenes (this is HBO, after all), but these complaints are to some degree born out of the premise, of the dwelling on the relationship between these two very different men (one of them old-school with misogynistic tendencies).

The first season of True Detective (****) is a rich, visually rewarding and structurally inventive story driven by outstanding performances and clever - if not developed fully - thematic ideas. There are also too many longueurs and moments of narrative stasis in a story that should really be unfolding with more verve and drive, but overall this is an impressive story. Whether Nic Pizzolatto can strike gold again with the forthcoming second season remains to be seen.ether Nic Pizzolatto can strike gold again with the forthcoming second season remains to be seen.

review_headline: Watch Prometheus first, then Noah and kind of keep track of both to see some corelations
review_body:
This movie was ok as a plot. I watched it right after watching Prometheus and found some correlation between the movies: An alien creator bringing life.

The giants in both Noah and Prometheus, are the Nephilim in the bible, that were on Earth to help man. Also, what I found interesting is the animal gatherings, that came in waves, but somewhat by species.

Though Noah's story can be a literal event, after watching Prometheus, it could be that Noah was a storage device for the species on the planet, before the last ice age melted, thus raising the waters around the world; or even an even more ancient, more dramatic ice age, interpretations could be many.

The increasing craziness of Noah, in my opinion, is an interpretation of fanaticism associated with religion and altruism, which is an oxymoron if you ask me.

Though the continuation of the human species from an incest DNA pool is highly questionable, overall the movie was great visually and philosophically.

product_title: Fifty Shades Freed: Book Three of the Fifty Shades Trilogy (Fifty Shades of Grey Series) (English Edition)
review_headline: The third just as poorly written as the first two, but still entertaining!
review_body:
Now that I've read the third in the Grey series, I can officially say, \\"I'm done with 50 Shades, for good!\\" It's definitely one of those book series that is so poorly written and constructed, but it's a guilty pleasure and I just couldn't help but wonder about the characters and their fates! I also see the appeal of the series to the millions of readers who have succumbed to the books--it's hard not to like the idea of a male who adores everything his wife does and thinks she is perfect in every way.

In Fifty Shades Freed, Ana and Christian are now married and learning to live with the other's quirks and flaws. But of course, several dramatic turns in the plot threaten their happily ever after. I found the book to be as unbelievable as the second book. Things just didn't add up--Christian completely altered his personality in such a short time, now becoming the perfect husband, with almost no domineering tendencies to speak of? I was entertained by Ana's inner critic, who is pretty amusing. I would only recommend reading this third in the series if you enjoyed the first two books, or if, like me, you couldn't help but be curious about how the characters' stories would end. This book also has a small section at the end called \\"Shades of Christian,\\" which allows the reader a glimpse into the beginning of the first book from Christian's point of view--interesting to read.

Some friends, who refuse to watch any sci-fi shows but this one, recommended it to me. At first I was suspicious, but after about the 4th episode I had decided that this was a very good show. I like the idea of a space western (star trek was supposed to be one, but instead opted for something more intelligent...) that is done in an interesting and intelligent manner. The characters are strong, and the way they develop and interact over the unfortunately brief 14-episode run is great.
The premise of a 'darker' future devoid of ANY alien races, poverty, and earth ruled corruptly is interesting and done pretty well. I also like the idea of our heroes being amoral thieves.
However, there is also a core of people (some of my friends among them) who are making the bold claim that this is greatest and best sci-fi show EVER. Of course, the people saying that have not seen any sci-fi shows but this one. There's nothing that makes this the best show ever, by any means.
The storylines, for example, are nice and develop the characters well. However, they aren't the most original, and if you've seen much of any Star Trek for example, you'll realize that these do resemble some things done before.
Just a word of advice, don't listen to the chorus of people saying \\"Firefly is much better than Star Trek\\" (who coincidentally have not ever seen more than 1 episode of any Star Trek series.) If you've seen a good deal of the four Star Trek shows (Enterprise not included of course) or Babylon 5 you'll enjoy this, but will most definitely not be shocked by the plotlines or proclaim it \\"the best show ever.\\" Instead, approach this show with an open mind, and you'll most likely be somewhat surprised by it and enjoy it.
Also, the Serenity movie is also quite good, but again, it's not exactly \\"the best show ever.\\"

review_headline: Read Oedipus Rex then Kafka on the Shore
review_body:
This was the most bizarre Murakmi novel I have ever read. That said, I loved it. I've heard a lot of criticism of this novel from normal Murakami book lovers, and I'd argue it's without merit. I admit it would be more difficult to understand if the reader has not read Oedipus Rex even though Murakami does a nice job of alluding to and summarizing much of the plot throughout the novel. Because it's such a strong plot and one of the lynch pins of psychoanalysis, the reader would benefit from having an awareness of the storyline before reading Kafka on the Shore.

Readers need to remember that one of Murakami's continual motifs is the way he plays with our perception of reality; he does this in almost every story. In this way, Kafka is able to use his imagination to heal from some of the trauma of his past. Whether or not the characters are who he thinks they are is not important, he assigns a new reality to the mother and sister figures for his own purpose. The power lies in the imagination, which Murakami would argue (through each of his novels) is reality itself.

review_headline: Breaking Dawn will ruin your entire view of the series.
review_body: Let me first say that I was another excited fan girl waiting with trepidation at midnight to get my pre-ordered copy of Breaking Dawn. I avoided all spoilers because I wanted to experience the book the way Stephenie Meyer intended, without any idea of what was going to happen. I wish I did know so I could prevent wasting my time and money on Breaking Dawn, or as it should be more aptly titled, Breaking Down. This book had so much potential to wrap up the series in a satisfying and interesting way and instead, the more I read, the more I was horrified at the book that was masquerading as a part of my favorite series. This book completely sullied an otherwise enthralling (though at times shallow) series.    (Spoilers below, read at your own risk.)  I suppose I should start with the sheer idiocy that was Bella's pregnancy. I completely agree with the reviewer that said that even in a fantastical and supernatural world, the events still need to adhere to the canon and rules previously set up in the Twilight universe. That's what keeps things realistic and that's what makes a successful series-- think Harry Potter (perhaps Ms. Meyer needs to take a page from Rowling's book. Not literally, of course). The fact that that Breaking Dawn is THEMED around a concept that Meyer has previously stated impossible ruins whatever believability the series had. Twilight has now become an AU fanfiction, plain and simple. Meyer has said that vampires can't even produce their own saliva, let alone fertile sperm that apparently has the ability to conceive life. I'm still waiting for an explanation of this phenomenon that makes sense and follows the Twilight canon, because honestly, are we expected to believe that this happened because Edward and Bella are just so different? Please.    Everything that happened in the book was so convenient. That's not the mark of a good writer, that everything can be explained by some fantastic loophole so that everything can be tied up in a pretty box witha bow. I'm pretty sure the general consensus of fans is that they want something realistic, not mindlessly inane and perfect. It's pretty convenient that Bella is somehow able to completely skip the newborn vampire stage because she's unique. What, pray tell, Ms. Meyer, is so different and special about Bella that she is the only person in thousands of years to be able to do this? Because frankly, all I've seen of Bella is a whiny, dependent, immature girl that is unable to think or live for herself. And how convenient that Jacob gets his own \\"happy ending\\" by imprinting on Nessie (yes, Nessie), the daughter of the girl that he's in love with. Because, discarding the pure yuck factor of that situation, if he can't have Bella, he might as well have the next best thing! And again, sheer convenience that Nessie grows at twice the normal rate, so that Jacob doesn't have to suffer with being a pedo for too long!    The morals Ms. Meyer presents us with in this novel are astounding. She's conveying that it's okay to get married (I'll give her that one) and have children at 18 because, hey, it's for love. And don't worry if you're too selfish or irresponsible to actually have another being be dependent on you, because everything will just work out fine! Forget discovering your own independence, forget college, forget your family and friends, it's worth it to be a teenage mother to a demon half-child. Thanks for the message, Smeyer!! I've discarded the sexist undertones of the series before this, because I was really hoping Bella would gain some sort of independence and original thought in this book. I was waiting for her to grow up. Don't expect it to happen. Bella's existence still revolves around a man and the story opens with Bella despairing, still, that she's not pretty enough, smart enough, anything enough, for the perfection that is Edward. We GET it, Stephenie, she's insecure! Can you actually develop her personality a little now?    Bottom line, this book is justtrash. The writing is sloppy (how many times do we have to hear Edward described as \\"perfect\\", \\"smooth as marble\\", and \\"icy to the touch\\" or read cheesy prose like, \\"Our gazes locked for a moment; his golden eyes were so deep that I imagined I could see all the way into his soul. He had the most beautiful soul, more beautiful than his brilliant mind or his incomparable face or his glorious body\\"), the characters aren't quite right, and the entire series does a total 180.    This series has gone downhill since New Moon, but please, if you value your sanity, end it with Eclipse. I want to ask Stephenie Meyer what she was thinking, but moreso, I want to know how this mindless garble made it past the editor's desk.

review_headline: Really well written with a few issues
review_body:
For the most part, this book was great and lived up to my expectations of a sequel to The Hunger Games, and I will still definitely be reading Mockingjay in the near future.

I've heard and read a lot of complaints about the love triangle between Katniss, Peeta, and Gale (though unless Peeta and Gale are considering a relationship with each other, I suppose it really isn't a triangle, but anyway), and usually that sort of thing doesn't interest me; but in the context of this book, and especially in the way Katniss at least considers the third option of remaining single because she never wants to have children who might be forced to participate in the Games, it wasn't a turn off for me. A *lot* of focus is put on this relationship drama, especially in the first half of the book, but since Katniss is not a drama queen and Collins is such a good writer, I didn't really get sick of it.

I can suspend my disbelief, in this book and the previous one, enough to believe that each District has been subdued enough by the Capitol to allow their children to be sent to the Hunger Games each year. What I can't believe though is the way Katniss acts when...

***MAJOR SPOILERS***

... she returns to the games and starts pretty much offing, or trying to off, people when she's been so disgusted and traumatized by the Games and the deaths and punishment of others previously. Collins tries to explain this away by Katniss thinking Peeta's the only good one of the bunch, with her and the other tributes just built to kill basically, but it doesn't jive. Also, there did not seem to be any good reason that she and Peeta were not trusted to know what was going on with the rebellion, especially in light of the facts that Katniss thought about and tried to kill people who might've been important, and she just happened to be in the right place at the right time and to intuit what to do to pull off their escape without knowing anything that was going on. That is way too much coincidence to ignore.

First off, this book isn't about a clown. I can't get anyone who has seen the mini-series to believe me. I realized when I re-read this that I had derived one very powerful parenting lesson from it over 20 years ago: don't lie to your children. That lesson comes from Eddie Kaspbrack. I also realized why small towns make my hair stand on end. I learned that from the old man who goes back inside his house. Re-reading this book made me realize that Stephen King is incredibly intuitive about what motivates people, what people fear, and how much we really lose when we decide to grow up. The side stories about the town make your guts clench because you know that in some small town somewhere, they are true. Horrors are inflicted upon neighbors without any supernatural help at all. THAT'S what makes this story so much more horrifying. Remove 'IT' and the story still stands on its own. The spiritual aspects of this book as as surprising as they are completely appropriate. I will warn you, though, if you are the kind of adult that believes that all children are innocent until 18 and should be kept that way, this book will probably offend you and you will refuse to believe that children can, will, and often do any of the things in the story. However, as an adult who actually remembers the truth of my childhood, there are extremes but nothing I didn't at least see a hint of as a kid. I highly recommend, as I think it is my most bookmarked e-book in my Kindle.

review_body:
I would like to assume that if you are reading this (MHO) review on this highly unusual DVD of Julia Fischer, you already know who Julia Fischer is and no further introduction is necessary..

For the benefit of those (just in case) who do not know Julia Fischer, she is known as one of the very best virtuoso violinist of our time. She is so talented that during the recording of Vivaldi Four Seasons Concerto in 2002, Sir Neville Mariner handed over his baton to Julia Fischer, and said to her that,\\"You don't need me here\\", then let Ms. Fischer to become the youngest person ever to lead \\"The-St.-Martin-In-The-Fields\\".

So, let's get into this incredible DVD. It was recorded live on January 1st, 2008 in Frankfurt, DE as the New Year's concert.

Ms. Julia Fischer has not played Saint-Saëns famous Violin Concerto no. 3 for about ten years. Although Ms Fischer had not played it for such a long time, and this is according to herself (this comment is in this DVD), it is because she believed that she had really \\"over-played\\" it. However, when she performs this Concerto again, she gave us her new perspective with mayurity on the violin concerto, this alone is worth the price of admission on this DVD. It is absolutely Julia : Sensitive, articulate and lyrical. Simply gorgeous.

The twist is, on that night, after the intermission, she shocked and pleased the audience with her Edvard Grieg's Piano Concerto in A minor. To be honest, it wasn't on par with world's \\"greatest\\" Grieg Piano Concerto performance, yet it was perfectly under control and she put out quite a few of the better known players to shame, However, that's not her point. She is a violinist that \\"thinks\\" in piano!

Conversely, we can ask ourselves, how many of those great pianists can play a convincing violin concerto without even the time for a proper rehearsal or practice? Probably none! How did she do it? Well, you will find this out on this DVD, which could put a smile on your face. Something that is very rare these days.

review_headline: So Satisfying! A Brilliant Book That Feels LIke A Throwback to Classic Kid Lit
review_body:
Brief Description: It is the late 1970s in New York City, and sixth grader Miranda has some big things to deal with: the sudden distance of her former best friend Sal, her mom's preparation for an upcoming appearance on The $20,000 Pyramid, and arrival of mysterious notes that predict events in Miranda's life before they actually happen. As Miranda struggles to cope with Sal's coldness, the mysterious notes begin to take on an element of danger. Miranda comes to believe that she must prevent a tragic death ... if only she could figure out what was going on and what she is supposed to do!

My Thoughts: I just fell in love with this book! When reading, it took me right back to my tween years, and I knew this was a book that I would have read and reread at age 10 or 11. In fact, with the 1970s setting, it felt like a book that had been written when I was a tween. At times, I almost felt like I had read this book in my childhood as it had a really specific feel to it that reminded me of two of my all-time favorite books from childhood, From The Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler and Harriet The Spy.

I think the feeling of familiarity is that Miranda is living in the real world but is experiencing a \\"secret\\" life that has fantastical elements to it. In other words, it is a fantasy book that takes place in the real world. These type of books always appeal to me because they make me think something similar might actually happen to me. (To this day, I cannot be in a museum without thinking of hiding in the bathrooms and living there like Claudia and Jamie in The Mixed-Up Files.) It also felt familiar because Miranda's favorite book is Madeline L'Engle's A Wrinkle In Time (which is referenced countless times and is part of the plot). A Wrinkle In Time was one of my favorite books too, and this shared loved of Meg and Charles Wallace and tesseracts helped me relate even more to Miranda.

Suggestion For Reading The Book: Find a smart 10- or 11-year-old kid who likes to read. Get both of you a copy of A Wrinkle In Time and When You Reach Me. Read the books together and discuss. Or, if this isn't possible, read the book yourself and enjoy being carried away by great children's literature. Whatever you do, just read this book!likes to read. I constantly found myself (every single chapter) flipping back to see who was supposed to be the one speaking during the dual narration of the third book. Tris and Tobias' characters totally changed here! Where was Four??? The tattooed hottie who was strong and distrusting? The one who protected Tris as much as she would allow? Tobias was a smart guy...surely he would have accompanied Tris to see Tris' brother Caleb to his death knowing she would do something stupid? And Four NEVER would have fallen apart over something as insignificant as finding out he wasn't as pure as Tris...give me a break. I gained zero insight from Tobias' point of view, and it was obvious to me as soon as I opened the book, the only purpose for the dual narrative was because Tris would die at some point. My biggest complaints are Tobias' checking out and becoming a complete pansy and I felt like the relationship between Tris and Tobias NEVER went anywhere. Tris sucked as Tobias' girlfriend! So many times I thought she should find him, comfort him, thank him, hug him...something! Anything! The relationship was totally one sided from the start. It was stupid. Secondly, Tris dies for no reason. To save the brother who betrayed her? The brother she could barely stand to look at? And for what really? To leave Tobias alone? The one who has given himself to her completely and who obviously needed her much more than she needed him? As many other reviews have stated, Tris' death was forced and unnecessary. review_headline: An intelligently and well written action thriller with a tremendously exhilarating, totally gripping story.
review_body:
No doubt many will read this (and the other Bourne books) because they've enjoyed the movie(s). As with the films, this book is incredibly intense, complicated and action packed. But it's far more than a potential screenplay. The stories bear almost no comparison at all, the films being only loosely based on the general (brilliant) concept and main character ... and of course the dramatic opening scene of this book.

The writer creates atmosphere perfectly. Where his passages are descriptive (of environment, emotion or event), he keeps it taut and relevant - enhancing without weighing down the progress of the narrative.

The action scenes are visceral, super-fast and, at times, brutal. Often coldly efficient and compact, as I imagine would be the case in the incredible urgency of a desperate, adrenalin fired battle to the death. Our hero acts on instinct, using his intrinsic skills, and is often confused by and even fearful of his extraordinary abilities.

The dialogue is precise and constructed in a way that feels real - although quite stiff and dated at times. This doesn't obstruct enjoyment of the book however and was probably right for the time it was written. There's an awful lot of \\"My darling\\" and \\"My true love\\" between Bourne and Marie (pretty much replaced by \\"babe\\" and \\"hun\\" now!)

One point that I was curious about: on three occasions the same unusual phrase popped up from sources of completely different background. `Spoors in the forest' is used by a high class Paris fashion house owner, then a thirty year American CIA veteran, then Bourne himself. Surely such different people would have different phrases to express ... well, whatever spoors in the forest means!

We're often in Bourne's head. Listening to his thoughts and internal desperate battles keeps us most definitely on his side and is a good contrast to the external action of the unfolding story.

Perhaps Marie is just a little TOO cool in this crisis. As she goes from economics genius, very much grounded in the sedate academic world of economics and politics to courageously dealing with brutal international assassins, covert government teams (it seems everyone on the planet is after Bourne), gun fights, rapists and kidnappers, as well as cleaning out bullet wounds. And all in a beautiful red silk dress and high heels.

It's a story of many layers and depths and hidden corners. It races ahead ... and around, and back, and across, and ahead ... at dizzying speeds. Is he good? Is he bad? Which side is he on? How many sides are there? Who is he?

It's very exciting. I've no idea how much of it is feasible but who cares! review_headline: The least-thrilling Jack Reacher novel so far . . . fails to meet high standards
review_body: Lee Child's creation, Jack Reacher, has earned his legions of fans the hard way - through kicking butt and taking names.  He's a surprising combination of loner, warrior, and detective and gifted with a surprising talent for finding trouble.    Thanks to Child's twisted imagination, Reacher has met several diabolical characters in his wanderings.  Indeed, these villains are among the best features of these books.  But the villain in the twelfth Reacher novel just doesn't rise to the usual level.  And this makes for a rather boring Reacher tale.    To be fair, a relatively boring Jack Reacher novel is better than most thrillers.  But we must weigh expectations, and they just aren't met here.    This novel follows the usual plot-line.  The book starts out with a sinister death, Reacher shows up and gets involved in trying to figure out what is going on.  Along the way he breaks some bones and uses his gifted detective's mind to thwart the dastardly villain.  Along the way he drinks a lot of coffee and romances a Reacher Girl - a competent, clean, beautiful, no-nonsense woman who shares Reacher's sense of adventure.    In this book, Reacher wanders into the Colorado towns of Hope and Despair.  Despair is where the action is.  Reacher tries to order a cup of coffee and is set upon by four grown men who want to kick him out of town.  Nobody kicks Jack Reacher out of town - they just don't know it yet.  Reacher tries to figure out what's going on in the company town - owned by an End Times religious fanatic of a businessman.  He does so with the help of Vaughan, a gorgeous cop from Hope who has a dark, painful secret.    What ensues, unfortunately, is a lot of driving around, walking, scaling of walls, and talking.  This has to be one of the least action-filled Reacher novels.  Yes, it tries to be \\"about something\\" by bringing up Iraq, conscientious deserters, and duty, but ultimately the novel fails to satisfy. This book reminds me of when you drive for two hours to yourfavorite restaurant, craving your favorite dish, only to be told they have a new chef and he doesn't get it just right.    Here's hoping the prolific Child returns to form quickly - Reacher is too good a character to waste.

product_title: A Dance with Dragons (A Song of Ice and Fire)
review_body:
I have been a fan of this series for many years, but Dance with Dragons continues the downward trend that started in A Feast for Crows. There are many accurate and detailed reviews already written, so I'll keep it short. No spoilers below about specific plot points, just general comments:

The bad:
1) Poor characterizations of several main characters via the use of repetitive mottos and baffling decision making.

2) Excessive filler due to seemingly pointless subplots and descriptions of food.

3) Unlike the bold, daring storytelling of previous books, the author has inserted \\"escape hatches\\" into the story so major events can be undone. The result is a reading experience that is non-committal and empty.
4) Numerous cliffhangers and death reversals.

5) Everything about Meereen, from its loathsome people to Dany's story, is hell. There is one significant moment that occurs, but the journey to reach it is a difficult, boring slog.

The good:
1) Bran, Arya and Theon's storylines provide some meaningful progression.

2) Victarion's story may be is slow, but he has a certain charm that makes him a worthwhile addition from the crop of new characters introduced in A Feast for Crows.

3) The events concerning Cercei are a harsh, but compelling, read.

GRRM needs to surround himself with people who care about making the reader's journey interesting and rewarding in each book, and who have an eye towards reaching the ultimate goal - bringing a satisfying (but not necessarily saccharine) end to this series. Based on the evidence in this book, he is surrounded by incompetent editors and sycophants. I sincerely hope GRRM finds his way again, and I wish him well in his efforts, but for now I am doubtful this series can end in two books.

product_title: Cloud Atlas (Movie Tie-in Edition): A Novel
review_body:
Very much like the work of Tarantino, this novel displays a very large talent who has not yet found anything significant to say, and relies on \\"meta\\" devices and big ideas to impress the audience. It's hard to believe that this has been received as a serious and rather difficult novel, when it is nothing more than a few reasonably competent stories and a pretentious structure. \\"Black Swan Green,\\" a rich and surprising semi-autobiographical book about adolescence, is not perfect, but it establishes much better ground to consider Mitchell a serious writer, and not just a flashy entertainer.

I suppose one could produce a work which achieves what is said of this book--the linking of disparate narratives, in different genres, taking place in different eras, which somehow reflect on one another and build to a grand and overarching statement. But Mitchell doesn't come close to doing this. The main theme of \\"Cloud Atlas\\" is noir writ large: exploitation, violence, conspiracy. (This kind of paranoia has supported many major works of fiction, though whether it has enhanced them is another matter. ) Mitchell takes a long view of this grim idea: the development of \\"civilization\\" is a story of rapacity and evil and will lead to disaster. He develops this theme through six stories set in different eras that are \\"linked\\" through a few stylistic tics and narrative contrivances, and then shoehorned into a pointlessly pretentious ABCDEFEDCBA structure. The stories are neither as different as he implies (all but one are essentially good-guy/bad guy thrillers) nor as deep as he needs them to be. The book is not difficult to read (except for the excruciating middle section), but the reader's memory is taxed by the long interlude between parts one and two of each of the first five stories.

Three of the stories are close to very good, though they would have benefited from rethinking and revision. The letters from a rebellious young composer in the 1920s are beautifully written, and the novel brings music to life in an imaginative and unexpected way--Mitchell does for music what Joyce Cary does for painting in \\"The Horse's Mouth.\\" This section of \\"Cloud Atlas\\" seems closest to the author's real talents. But it evolves into an unconvincing account of unrequited love, and its tragic ending is inexplicable. Also, its plot and themes are so different from the other five stories that it is hard to tell why it is in this novel. The pulp eco-thriller set in the 1970s is a rather good example of its type, with reasonably well developed characters and well-executed double and triple crosses. It's the least pretentious and most successful of the six pieces. Mitchell could probably do this for a living, if he wanted to. The sci-fi narration about a dystopian future has an interesting premise, developed with clever detail and a lot of narrative drive; while it eventually wore out its welcome, I enjoyed most of it and was surprised by its surprise ending.

There is less to be said for the other three stories. The writing in the nineteenth-century South Sea narrative is decent pastiche, but the underlying plot and characters are unbelievable, and it makes its thematic points with a sledgehammer. The Amis imitation about a contemporary publisher trapped in a nursing home is a trivial jape, not very amusing, and its plot is absurd. There is some inventiveness to the central story, set in the far future, when advanced civilization has collapsed, and the survivors in Hawaii have reverted to tribalism, with memories of the past enshrined in myth. They receive a visitor from a more advanced society, echoing the first story in the South Seas, and again raising the specter of colonialism. Unfortunately the narrator is given a cloying sub-Faulknerian faux-naive voice that set my teeth on edge. I felt that I was in Dogpatch, not on the Big Island. A struggle to get through.

I suppose I ought to comment on thevarious ways in which these stories are linked through detail and motif and even plot to imply that the story of man is one big horrible story, but most of them are rather silly and mechanical. (There's a lot of talk about recurrence, and each story includes a character with a comet birthmark on the shoulder. Oy. ) Four stories do echo one another thematically--the eco-thriller and the three stories set in the past and the future--but if anything that trivializes them, giving you the feeling that Mitchell has found various ways to say the same thing.

\\"Cloud Atlas\\" has a secondary theme unrelated to its big idea--the perennial power of narrative in shaping our identity. Each of the stories except the last one is read in some way by a character in the next story in sequence. The two stories set in the future comment a lot on history and tradition. And there is a bit of explicit discussion about the art of narrative.

Mitchell is clearly a gifted storyteller, with a wide range of tools and an acute eye and ear. All of his tales move swiftly (they have to--they're quite short). Still, this novel vividly illustrates the downside of \\"story-telling\\" as a model for fiction: the piling on of coincidences and reversals, the assembly of various strands into a tidy ending, the failure to develop character because the plot takes priority, the use of gratuitous detail to enhance the \\"significance\\" of the story. Despite his skill with language, his encyclopedic knowledge and curiosity, his wit, his elan, Mitchell's work here tends to peter out, as plot contrivances take over. I started flipping pages to get to the end of each section. The same was true when I read his most recent novel, a tale of traders in Japan, which opens with a bang, sets the scene very well, and disintegrates into a distasteful and implausible suspense story.

Mitchell seems uneasily poised between the skills and aspirations of literary fiction and the methods of pulp and genre fiction. It will be interesting to see how he develops. When he's at his best, he can do anything. But on balance I was bored and disappointed by \\"Cloud Atlas.\\"

review_body: Enough people here had written that this was/is Leone's masterpiece so I had to see what I was missing. I've always considered the Good The Bad & The Ugly to be the best western I had ever seen and so there was good reason to check this out. Having read it is somewhat slow I wasn't expecting an action thriller but honestly the flick left me a bit (just a bit) disappointed. Honestly it comes off as very uneven to me. I recall reading somewhere that Morricone had written the soundtrack before Leone had actually filmed the scenes and that might explain why it just doesn't fit very well. It seems to be disjointed and doesn't paint a background for the picture that helps to hold it all together. It's missing a genuine ambiance to it which is something you can get away with on an album or audio CD but a movie, especially one with the expectations this had, should have something subtly holding the whole thing together. That's not to say the music is bad but it is lacking. The harmonica bit played for the Bronson character is a good concept but it falls short of inspiring any particular message or feeling. The banjo plays far too much and is both out of place, lame and a little annoying.     The Frank character played by Henry Fonda isn't particularly believable. His voice conveys too much human emotion for someone who is supposedly truly evil. I think Eastwood's character being next to expressionless both visually and vocally would have been more in keeping with this plot. That is unless Leone intentionally wanted this character to show more emotion in order to portray him as a psychopath but if that's thecase Fonda was still badly cast. He just doesn't come across as being deep enough or twisted enough to really inspire that sort of terror.     Claudia Cardinale is a real piece of eye candy but I somehow doubt that a woman who looked like that would have survived thirty seconds in the old west. Bronson's character smiles too much and I just get the impression the entire production was intent on playing to American audiences. Too many big names that didn't particularly suit their part. I also got the impression that Leone didn't have total creative control over the production or it's subtleties. Something about the entire thing comes across as too many chefs in the kitchen. Too much compromising and the film suffers from lack of a unified/single vision.    The cinematography is fantastic but everything about the scenes seem sterile and phony. It's all too clean and everything (the saloons, the kitchens, train cars...) are almost sterile and missing the sort of filth that makes his previous westerns seem real and personal.     This isn't a bad movie but all things considered I think it could have been a lot better.

While I've watched big screen adaptations of Hornby's books (High Fidelity, About A Boy) but had never actually read a Hornby book till Juliet, Naked. Although the book looks a bit long (almost 400 pages in hardback!) it was well worth it.

Annie and Duncan are in a relationship that is boring, stale, and a matter of convenience. Duncan is a Crowologist (an expert on everything Tucker Crowe), but past listening to a few of his songs, Annie doesn't really care about Tucker Crowe one way or another. Who is Crowe? Decades ago he used to be an up-and-coming star, but abruptly stopped performing, writing, and recording. Now, the only thing that fanatic, die-hard Tucker Crowe fans have are supposedly random sightings, and picking apart the meaning in his lyrics and performances. One day Duncan admits that he's been unfaithful to Annie, and their relationship abruptly ends, although Annie is not as sad or heart broken as she thought she should have been. In the middle of all this, she has posted a review of Crowe's latest release, a stripped down version of his last album, Juliet. Much to her surprise, she receives an email from Crowe.

Its not necessarily the plot that makes Hornby such a great writer, but the way he conveys his message, and the simplicity of his writing. The book will definitely resonate with readers, whether it be through Annie and Duncan's complacency in their relationship, the regret that Annie and Tucker both feel for having let so much time go to waste, or the fact that nobody seems to be doing what they love to do. This is one of the rare books I've read where I've finished and just sat around reflecting about my own life, and thinking about how I need to make some changes.

It might seem like a light read, but in the end, the themes and messages conveyed are very thought provoking. Great novel!

Tim Burton's 90's classic \\"Nightmare Before Christmas\\" used state-of-the-art stop-motion animation/claymation and told the story of Jack Skellington, a bony skeleton King of Halloween Land who orders the kidnap of Santa Claus from Christmas Land in order that he delivers toys for Christmas for one year. The satire within the story can be appreciated by adults. It seems to criticize the commercialism of Christmas and in its twisted way, it works. It is also the story of Jack Skellington's dreams and he is seen as a kind of hero by the end of the movie. For its time, this movie was innovative. The creations - ghouls, goblis, skeletons, witches, vampires and other Halloween creatures- come to life vividly on screenand appear as human as the rest of us. The songs are very catchy. Who can forget Skellington belting out \\"What's this ?\\" and the chorus song \\"This Is Halloween\\". Tim Burton pulls all the stops and this bizarre film is nothing unusual for the bleak style that Burton's films are famous for (Edward Scissor Hands, etc). The only other similar stop-animation film that took Burton years to make is the recently released Corpse Bride, which unfortunately didnt do so well in theaters. It is still a good film but it lacks the depth, characterization and good storytelling that Nightmare has. I hope that when Corpse Bride is released on DVD, there will be mention of Nightmare Before Christmas.

Glenda Findley said it best, \\"we were all young once, try looking at this movie through the eyes of an 8 year-old\\". Don't ever believe because you age, your inner child must fade away. The newest reviews, stated that there was too much emotional or mental bagage...that's talk of narcissistic, self-righteous, over-zealous, egomaniacs, who are more or less likely not to keep in touch with their inner child, feelings, emotions or the sensitivity of others. I couldn't disagree MORE! It is because of the emotional/mental torment that makes these characters so lovable and easy to relate to. I agree, there were many clichés, and \\"one-liners\\" used time and time again in this crazy Western popular culture of ours...but remember that this is simply entertainment: take it for what it is and nothing more!
The special effects were spectacular, and as explained in the Bonus DVD are wonderfully executed, thought-out and well planned. This movie does deliver the best eye candy I've seen in a while, in terms of special effects. And it was thoroughly enjoyed by most.
I congratulate Guillero Del Toro, for staying as faithful as he possibly could to the comic book - which by the way is based on the \\"Seed of Destruction\\" series.
Although such characters like Abe Sapien (Doug Evans), Liz Sherman (Selma Blair) are not developed enough. I thought it wasn't necessary.(...)
Liz Sherman (for whatever reason's character and acting ability continues to be undermined by her beauty - again by crazy misogynists) represents the severely depressed, yet terribly intelligent, charming, compassionate and giving. Her abilities similar to Abe Sapien's, can only be accessed when they are heightened by emotions/feelings/energies. She is profound, an intellect, sensitive, a thinker, and independent of any one being: her full self. Her character although not fully developed is still essential to the story line. Let's remember that if we develop each and every character to such a wide extent that ALL MOVIES would take more than 4 hours + (remember Queen of the Damned). Her depression stems from the fact that she is a very profound intellect and detached of any selfishness, pride, ego, or superficial trappings. Her emotions/senses are the reasons why she can utilize her pyrokinetic abilities. This is because she has a deeper range of emotions, that connects her to all living things.
Ron Perlman, was brilliant as Hellboy. No other human being in the world could have played such a well-developed character. I couldn't imagine anyone else playing that role. It was made for him perfectly and he is stunning that makeup. No one else could have looked that well in \\"lobster\\" makeup. He delivers his performance brilliantly. Even those over-used \\"one-liners\\" seem brand new when said by Ron Perlman. Nothing to say except : Perfect Performance. A+++
John Hurt as Hellboy's \\"father\\" was a joy to watch as well. Like any father, he cares for his son...and raised him to do by right although Hellboy is \\"hell itself\\". Proving that we can all do away with that side of ourselves if we work hard at it.
Jeffrey Tambour as the boss, delivered the best performance he could, given the script he had to work with. The one thing I must mention about this character is that, often times, when he seemed perturbed by Hellboy's personality...it didn't quite \\"feel\\" right...it felt forced and was delivered simply as an \\"add on\\". His character is made to be believed by the audience that he will not be intimidated by a hell-born creature, that he will always be the \\"Boss\\" of everyone and no other man or creature for that matter could take his place! His character is suppose to represent the egomaniac, power-hungry-obsessed \\"boss\\" who doesn't give Hellboy a rest...but that doesn't quite flush out perfectly enough!
The cinematography is enjoyable for the most part. The pacing is reasonably well. The only thing that needed work for themost part are the villains. They had to be a thousand times for threatening...even the monsters Sammael are not demonic enough to frighten anyone in any subway! I believe, all in all, that the villains needed the most development as characters...but everything else is just fine.
What's best about this action super-hero/heroine movie is that the characters are FLAWED, that's what makes them so special and unique and more importantly human. Hellboy is madly in love with Liz, but terribly insecure when Agent Myers spends time with her for a coffee on a bench, even goes as far as throwing a small rock at his head! That was delightful...even the conversation he carries with the 9 year-old boy. It shows that beneath that machochistic exterior, there really is a wonderful Hellboy inside. All of these characters (except the villains of course), have inner demons to deal with...even Father has an ailing heart that he refuses to reveal to his son, in fear of making him upset. It's the humanity in these characters that makes them so easy to relate to...Superman and Spiderman are superficial garbage...with little or no substance...Superman comes from another planet...I can hardly relate to that. And I wouldn't want to. If being perfect and well thought out, is being selfish, an over-zealous egomaniac, with little concern for others except yourself, then don't watch this movie because by that definition, this movie would surely suck!
I love seeing that these are not your typical \\"heroes\\", they are imperfect and it's the flaws that make people perfect and strive to make people better themselves...to be perfect, which doesn't even exist, logically, then there really would be no point in living. But striving to achieve perfection, gives you meaning and purpose to your life and something worth thinking about.
They don't even look like your typical heroes. It's wonderful to see an \\"X-File research an X-File\\" or as other people have mentioned \\"X-Men meets the X-Files\\"...there's an original idea. This movie just explains Hellboy's origins, and what he's about. The sequel will, no doubt, offer more in terms of plot. I remember the first X-Men wasn't anything much, because so much of it, just explained their origin and what they were. It's the same with this movie. And it is the best thing we've seen this year so far (considering how deplorable movies have become over the years).
The Bonus DVD includes wonderful features, from commentary to deleted scenes, to Mike Mignola's explanation of his original creation...it was wonderful.
Great effects, well enough plot, reasonable pacing and cinematography, developed characters with the exception of the villains...but over all, different, unique, and certain a different take on superheroes.
By the way: The big hand is a Stone Hand. He never really uses it for what it's made for because Hellboy was raised by humans. The Stone Hand is used to unlock the \\"portal\\" to set Behemoth free of its crystal prison. In the human world, he just uses it to smash things.
The most unforgettable thing is the relationship between Hellboy and Liz...they did after all grow up together as \\"freaks\\" of the Bureau of Paranormal Research and Defense as children. Her \\"power\\" is pyrokinesis, and he is fire-proof. It's no wonder they are the perfect match. I wonder what their children would be like \\"half-hellish half-human\\"....
The most important thing I've learned from this movie is that our imperfections make us who we are. As far as I'm concerned, to have no \\"baggage\\" at all, is to experience nothing and to learn nothing...and to agree to refuse to \\"disconnect\\" and remain ego-centric. Sure, \\"baggage\\" has to flush out, but new \\"baggages\\" must arrive at the airport some time soon, giving us reasons to exist and to learn and to grow. It's a continual process...I liked that these heroes were not \\"clean-cut\\" or the stereotypes of what heroes are supposedly meant to be.
Can't wait for the sequel!

product_title: The Troubled Man: A Kurt Wallander Mystery (10)
review_body: The worst part of this final Wallander is the last couple of paragraphs, where Mankell makes certain that his agent or his bank account, if it becomes depleted, won't pressure him into writing another in the series. The image that precedes those final paragraphs is stark and sufficient, much better for closure than what he decides to do, apparently in a fit of pique. That wasn't necessary, Henning.    If a good crime novel holds a mirror up to society, then this one brings to light how Sweden enabled the U.S. to do as it wished in Swedish territory during the Cold War because Sweden saw the Soviet Union, reasonably enough, as the true threat. While Mankell's staccato style hasn't changed, and while Wallander is as persistent as ever, the detective at 60 is a physical wreck who endures bouts of forgetfulness that become more and more pronounced. The best parts of the book deal with family. Wallander says that he has neglected to cultivate his friendships, and here he lives with the consequences; the case he pursues involves a former naval commander and his wife, who are the parents of Wallander's daughter's new romantic partner. His daughter Linda, also a cop when she's not on maternity leave, is determined to get her father to shape up.     Though Wallander has a dog and treats him well, he is otherwise surly and even unsavory in this final installment in the distinguished series. Death haunted, he faces his own personal failures without any consolations: no wife or romantic partner, few if any real friends, little interest in literature or music or even travel, just a deep restlessness and despair. Though the procedural details are as fascinating as ever, this is not primarily a book about solving a crime or finding redemption. Instead, it's a cautionary tale that will leave you feeling depressed. It doesn't pull its punches, but then neither does life as we age.    I would have wished a better fate for Wallander, but he's Mankell's man. This somber novel unrelieved by any antic fun or celebration is honest.

review_headline: Supertramp's live document from 1979 is MAGNIFIQUE!
review_body:
Supertramp's seventh album entitled Paris was released in October of 1980.
Now, a Blu-Ray (and DVD) has been released of the classic Supertramp performances from Paris in December of 1979 called Supertramp Live in Paris 1979.
The film was shot and recorded in December of 1979 in Paris, France at the Pavillion on the penultimate night of the band's Breakfast in America European tour. Supertramp Live in Paris is a superb concert film, capturing the band at the peak of their popularity when co-leader/guitarist/singer/keyboard player/songwriter Roger Hodgson was still with the group. When you consider that the possibility of Hodgson returning to Supertramp these days very doubtful, Paris becomes an extremely important live document of the classic lineup of the band, indeed. This concert film had been fabled for years and no footage had been officially released (aside \\"The Logical Song\\" and \\"Dreamer\\" as promo films) it wasn't until the master tapes of the December 1, 1979 performance were discovered in drummer Bob Siebenberg's barn in cow dung. Then longtime producer Peter Henderson and old concert sound engineer Russell Pope (whom produced the original album) painstakingly restored and transferred the audio from analog to digital and brilliantly mixed the audio. Then Peter Clifton (the same man who finished Led Zeppelin's The Song Remains the Same after Joe Massot bailed) salvaged the footage shot by Derek Burbidge (who filmed much of The Police's promo videos in the day) and added some bits to round out the film. What is available is a superb document of the classic Supertramp lineup.
Many great Supertramp classics are included in this live concert film, such as most of 1974's grand breakthrough Crime of the Century (the spirited opener \\"School\\", a slightly extended \\"Bloody Well Right\\", an excellent \\"Hide in Your Shell\\", a superb \\"Asylum', the Top 20 hit \\"Dreamer\\", a superb \\"Rudy\\" and the closing \\"Crime of the Century\\" which closes this live concert film), two songs from 1975's highly underrated followup Crisis? What Crisis? (\\"Another Man's Woman\\" and \\"Two of Us\\" both superior to studio versions), three from 1977's Gold selling US breakthrough Even in the Quietest Moments (the title cut, \\"Give a Little Bit\\" and the best version of \\"Fool's Overture\\" ever which has an ending that is to be seen to believe), and half of the #1 Multi-Platinum selling Breakfast in America (the monster hit \\"The Logical Song\\", the hit \\"Goodbye Stranger\\", the title cut, the Top 20 smash \\"Take The Long Way Home\\" and the epic closer \\"Child of Vision\\").
Hodgson and co-leader/keyboardist/singer/songwriter Rick Davies sing their hearts out and play their respective keyboards with great passion, and Hodgson also serves up some incredible fretwork on the guitar. Co-horts John Helliwell on saxophones/clarinets/occasional keyboards and additional backing vocals, drummer Bob C. Benberg and bass player Dougie Thomson have terrific interplay with Hodgson and Davies, helping to bring the band's great melodic music to life in tremendous fashion. Just like on their studio albums, the band totally cook live in concert, too. The songs on here rival their studio counterparts, especially on Rudy which is sped at faster speed than the studio version on the Roger/Rick vocal duel section and the visuals of the backdrop films are superb.
The songs that weren't shot for the film which were recorded (\\"Ain't Nobody But Me\\", \\"You Started Laughing\\", \\"Downstream\\", \\"A Soapbox Opera\\" and \\"From Now On\\") are here as bonus tracks with visuals created specifically for the DVD/Blu-Ray.
Also, much to Roger Hodgson's chagrin, the songwriting credits are printed on the back of the Blu-Ray (may not have been there on the first issue) and the Supertramp fans are just grateful that this classic document of the band's peak is FINALLY AVAILABLE!!!
Highly recommended!), two songs from 1975's highly underrated followup Crisis? What Crisis? product_title: The End of Faith: Religion, Terror, and the Future of Reason
review_body:
Dr. Harris' book is basically--not entirely, but basically--an extended rant against Islam. While he has a valid point about the theoretical dangers of religious fanaticism in all faiths, his evidence focuses almost exclusively upon Islamic suicide bombers. Dr. Harris chooses to ignore, for example, \\"Christian\\" abortion clinic bombers and murderers. He also chooses to ignore--or at least gives very short shrift to--the fact that the unreasonable belief of fundamentalist Christians and Jews--that some mythical \\"god\\" supposedly \\"gave\\" the Middle East to a nomadic band of sheep and goat herders three thousand years ago and that this \\"gift\\" entitles their descendants to walk in and take over after a two thousand year absence--has caused far more misery and death than a few Islamic terrorists ever have. He also chooses to ignore that the fundamentalist Christians are doing their best to bring about Armageddon--the end of the planet, through nuclear holocaust, if necessary--and that even at their most intolerant and extreme the Islamic terrorists aren't going for world destruction.

I also have a problem with Dr. Harris' apparent belief that the West in general, and the USA in particular, are somehow morally superior to the Islamic people. It is true that by cherry-picking quotations from the Koran and from the Jewish/Christian Bible, one can make the case that Islam is a more violent religion than either Judaism or Christianity (and, I might add even though Dr. Harris wouldn't, the obverse is also true). But the record shows differently--the proof is in the pudding, as they say. For centuries, Muslims lived in peace with the Jews; Christians slaughter them. Hitler, after all, was a Catholic--never excommunicated--and the Catholic Church participated willingly in the Holocaust. Need I mention the Crusades, or the rapacious treatment of the \\"New\\" world by invading Jesuits, Dominicans, etc., or the \\"Christian\\" West's colonial policies?

Even more appalling is Dr. Harris' moral blindness when it comes to specifically American actions. He excuses the American bombing, in 1998, of a pharmaceutical plant in Sudan on the ground that we mistakenly thought it was an Al-Qaeda facility and, after all, \\"we meant well.\\" Dr. Harris, I was always thought that if people of good will make a mistake they rectify the situation as best they can by reparing the damage and by compensating the victims of their mistakes. As far as I know, we have never even apologized for--let alone set right--the disastrous consequences of our \\"honest mistake.\\" Too, Dr. Harris, ignoring the larger question of morality in our invasion, goes to great lengths to assert (on faith, apparently, because he presents no evidence but simply parrots the Shrub's propaganda line)the extreme efforts the USA has gone to be gentle in its rape of Iraq. Failing to pay attention to our routine use of torture, the author seems to think that we should win points because our soldiers cry after they gun down innocent civilians. This is like going into a man's house, beating him to a pulp, making him watch while you rape his wife and daughter, stealing his money, and then claiming the moral high ground because you felt sorry for it later.

Invading vietnam & killing upwards of a million of its citizens, carpet bombing, chemical warfare,My Lai? Forget about it--our soldiers were \\"horrified\\" by it; never mind that nothing was ever done to anyone in the chain of command, except for one hapless lieutenant--besides, \\"our intentions were good.\\" Terror bombing of Dresden, Hiroshima, and Nagasaki? Dr. Harris gives these terrorist acts by the \\"Christian\\" West no mention. From 1945 Hiroshima to 2005 Guantanamo, the USA has either committed or supported one terrorist atrocity after another--so many that it is safe to say that the leading terrorist nation in the world is the USA. Islamic terrorism pales in comparison. Yet, since \\"our intentions are good\\"--again a beliefthat Dr. Harris apparently holds on faith since we have no evidence for it--we are morally superior to a bunch of raghead fanatics who are giving their bodies so that their people might be free of foreign domination to be left in peace.

Dr. Harris asks us--rhetorically, I suppose--whether Iraqi soldiers would be as \\"nice\\" to the civilian population in the USA as we have to Iraq's. On no evidence whatsoever--again on the faith Dr. Harris decries--we are left to conclude that the Islamists, who apparently never mean well, are savages. He fails to draw the obvious conclusion: that his rhetorical device is absurd. Iraq would never invade the USA--countries only invade those that are vastly weaker than they, the USA against Granada, Panama, and the Dominican Republic come to mind.

Anyway, racism, classism, moral snobbery, and a too-easy apologia for US terrorism aside, Dr. Harris makes some good points. Religious fanatics--Christian and Jewish at least as much as Islamic--ARE the number one threat to human survival, and Dr. Harris appropriately sounds the alarm. There's also some good information on how the brain works and how beliefs are formed. That is why this book gets two stars instead of one.

product_title: The Troubled Man: A Kurt Wallander Mystery (10)
review_headline: One of the best books I have ever read. A stunner of a mystery as well as a portrait of not one but two troubled men
review_body:
I absolutely could not put this book down until I'd finished it and wish I could give it far more than 5 stars. It is rare to find an extremely well-written book which blends an intriguing international mystery with such compelling characterizations, particular that of Wallender, his daughter, and a retired naval commander.

If you're familiar with Mankell's series about Swedish detective Kurt Wallender, you'll want to grab this one as soon as possible. If not, you can certainly start with The Troubled Man (although I'd suggest you read the books in order).

I'm often not a fan of international spy thrillers but Kurt Wallander is a compelling man, a thoughtful and often somber person whose concerns tugged at my heart - his sense of mortality and other fears about himself (I can't list more details without adding spoilers) as well as his relationships with the women in his life, past and present.

Wallender's feelings about those women are complex and ambivalent. Wallender has an often prickly connection to his daughter and she has her own judgments of her father, even forcing him into situations that make him uncomfortable. Then there is Haken Von Enke, a retired naval commander who confesses just enough about an international incident to make Wallender determined to discover the truth. That is the mystery which is the focus of this book.

The title is perfect because it covers more than one \\"troubled man\\". Of course there is Von Enke, who probably wouldn't have confided in Wallender if he hadn't been so upset but there is also Wallender himself.

So there are actually two troubled men as well as excellent writing which ramps up the suspense page by page....resulting in a book which should leave readers satisfied and even stunned by Mankell's skill as an author. I intend to read this one again -and perhaps again after that - because I'm sure I have just begun to tap into the rich, multi-layered world created by Mankell.

There are also philosophical questions raised by Mankell, ones that are likely to resonate with readers, and I had to put the book down to think about how I felt about Wallender's challenges - and similar ones in my own life.

The last few pages of The Troubled Man left me reeling. In a relatively short amount of space, Mankell created a poignant ending and I was moved to tears.

This movie works in more ways than I can even think to name. Start with the start power: Leonardo DiCaprio in the lead role, Ellen Page playing the most mature part I've seen so far, an under-used Michael Caine, Ken Watanabe, and more.

The action plays out in the dreams of the heir to an industrial empire. The goal: to get him to shut it down. Despite the obvious risk of degenerating into psychobabble, this stays true to its action theme, even when levels of reality start to layer like pastrami on rye. The victim, it turns out, has unexpected defenses. The attacker, it turns out, has unexpected weaknesses. And Page's character, Ariadne, takes on the role of her mythic namesake in unwinding the labyrinths of architecture and mind - not that this movie makes clear distinction.

This could have become an effects-flick, as shown in Ariadne's intro to the dreamworld - possibly the most dramatic urban dreamscape since [[ASIN:0780622553 Dark City]]. That setpiece really just served to show the effectmeister's general restraint, except on the few scenes where the enhancement really mattered. Instead, the movie relies on plot, action, and acting - a refreshing change from so many summer films of recent years.

The multi-reality backdrop worked well, on the whole, but might become clearer on a second viewing. No matter. \\"Inception\\" works well as a summer popcorn movie, but works well at other levels too. For once, it's a summer movie I'll remember even when summer is gone.

Yet as I read, I quickly realized it is so much more than a murder mystery. This is a really important book. Moriarty does a fine job of developing three main characters - all women, and capturing their strengths and insecurities so that I could not help but relate, understand, and love them. Most importantly, this book addresses something that is both very wrong and very prevalent in society, and that is also very difficult to talk about. Many women will find the violent circumstances all too relatable, and yet most real-life violence comes to much different conclusions than in this book. Still, I hope reading this gives women courage to speak up and find the support they need to get out of such circumstances. But as this book portrays, that is quite difficult to do.

Finally, I hardly noticed the writing as I was so immersed in the story. This, to me, indicates the writing was good enough that it didn't hinder my experience of the story. I'll be reading more by this author.

review_body:

product_title: One Summer: America, 1927 by Bryson, Bill (2013) Hardcover
review_headline: Immerse Yourself in 1927!  A Must-Read for History and Culture Junkies!!!
review_body:
Who thought history could be so interesting! In One Summer, Bill Bryson tells you a lot of facts regarding the early 20th century that you never learned in school. He weaves in information from earlier eras to demonstrate the mindset of 1927 America. Bryson covers popular culture of the time, including baseball and early film. The author has obviously done excellent research, citing details to cover every aspect of each topic. He makes the reader feel as if they were really experiencing 1927 America.

Bryson also covers social issues of the times, including crime, racism, and early 20th century terrorism on United States' soil-who knew? In addition to presenting information in an interesting fashion to the reader, Bryson helps the reader understand that every era has its own problems. Most people would think of 1927 as "the good old days," but Bryson helps us see that America experienced good times and bad times back then, just like today. I feel his message was one of optimism.

I came away realizing that people are always most disturbed about the problems that are right upon them-crime and unrest in 1927, World War II in the 1940s, the Cold War, Vietnam, 9-11, etc. We always feel the current problems are worse because the outcome is unknown. Bryson helped me appreciate that fact, in his own subtle way.

product_title: Professor Satchafunkilus and the Musterion of Rock
review_headline: It is what it says it is
review_body: Interestingly this is my first ever album review that I've done, and certainly the first on amazon; what can I say this is a Satch album after all ;)    As fair warning, I haven't heard the album extensively, so these are purely first impressions, but I'm going to make them as detailed as possible. I initially thought of avoiding the song by song analysis, but ended up going with it anyway. I'll try and offer a cohesive perspective on the album as a whole.    Professor Satchafunkilus and the Musterion of Rock    The album starts off with an ominous dark vibe as \\"Musterion\\" kicks off. To draw a comparison, it reminded me sort of the song \\"Belly Dancer\\" or \\"Oriental Melody\\" from the SBM album. There are definitely some interesting moments in the song, Satch's playing is quite twisted The song retains a format similar to most of Satch's \\"standard\\" more rock oriented songs - all in all an interesting album opener.    \\"Overdrive\\" continues almost where \\"Musterion\\" left off - however, it gives the listener the feeling of really settling into the album. Heavy rock-solid guitar arrangements over a pretty basic drum and bass groove. However the layering of guitar sounds really thickens up the mix, and Satch is playing those memorable hooks and big sounding chords! This is the first kind of \\"take notice\\" stereotypical Satch solo. A very pronounced minor tonality and some really nice melodies. A pretty guitar heavy and dramatic closure to the song leading straight into...    \\"I Just Wanna Rock\\" - whether a reference to the old Twisted Sister song, I don't know, but it is what it says it is. This is very similar to \\"Crowd Chant\\" off Super Colossal. Straight up bare bones rocker, which is spiced up by Satch using a Talk-Box - this is definitely going to be one for the audience.    And this is where things get real hip ~ from ZZ's dissonant tenor lines which segue into \\"Professor Satchafunkilus\\". It's all about the funk! Satch's layered melodic guitar lines pretty much tell the listener to get off the seat and move one's posterior on the downbeat. Very hip and funky, funkier than \\"The Snake\\" off his first album or \\"Cool#9\\". This is a real funky tune which I have no doubt Satch is going to use to build off to an Satchanormous jam when he plays it live! Some real sneaky and hip soloing going on there too and the song drops out to ZZ repeating his melodies - works just brilliantly.    and \\"Revelation\\". We could have done without this one. Nothing new here at all. Satch doing some soulful soloing over what sounds like a backing track. Without letting my feelings for Satch as one hip dude coming into the way, it's a pretty boring track. Nothing new here, though to its credit the song ends with some really nice soloing from Satch and picks up in intensity. But overall, disappointing given its name, anything but a revelation.    \\"Come on Baby\\" is the trademark love song that is there in every Satch album. Again, it is what is says it is. It has been done before, but there's some inventive and nice soloing in there, and the main melody is really nice almost 60ish hippie sounding.    \\"Out of the Sunrise\\" is yet again something that I personally could've done without on the album. It's pretty much like a nondescript 80s sounding track with Satch soloing on top of it, probably the lowest point of the album. Its only saving grace is when Satch breaks off into the solo halfway into the song, but it still ends with the hateful cheesy melody lines.    Thankfully Satch keeps it real by breaking into \\"Diddle-Y-A-Doo-Dat\\" with a real prog sounding intro in odd time with harmonized guitar lines which quickly segues into a down and dirty drum and bass groove. There's almost a nod to the Jeff Beck group in the way Satch explores the melodies. The shortest song in the album, it almost brings the listener back on track to let us know Satch means business. What's really unique about this song is the presence of a dirty organ arrangement - something that I've neverin the past 6 years of listening to Satriani, ever really heard!    And we're down to the last two songs on the album. Middle eastern percussions and an open stringed melody line lead into \\"Asik Vaysel\\" which is in my opinion the album's highlight. This is pure quintessential Satch doing his thing. The mystical intro leads into a straight up shred fest as only Satch can do it. Reminiscent of a live version of \\"Circles\\" in terms of song structure, but similar to \\"Surfing with the Alien\\" or \\"Flying in a Blue Dream\\" in terms of energy. Insane soloing and some great melodies and grooves.    \\"Andulasia\\" starts off in a similar manner, stripped down acoustic melodies interweaving through each other with some beautiful acoustic soloing before we get hit with this wall of transcendental guitar noise as the band kicks into full flow. Satch takes over the proceedings and blows you away like only he can. Great way to wrap up the album, you gotta listen to it to feel the energy and the vibe.    So that's about it for first impressions on the album. I'd give it a 4 out of 5 rating. The songs which stand out, definitely grab the listener and gets 'em involved into Satch's playing. However I could have done without the fillers in the album. It's not like they are bad songs, but Satch being Satch makes us have rather groovy expectations. However this album has great potential for repeat listens and though Satriani doesn't necessarily break new ground, he does his thing with panache and style. I had secretly hoped for Dave LaRue to be playing bass on the album rather than Matt Bissionette - I do NOT dig his bass playing, and Dave La Rue works incredibly well with Satch. So I was disappointed that Satch enlisted Matt Bissionette still. Therefore even though you have a drum powerhouse like Jeff Campitelli slamming the skins, the energy from the band is not at its optimum. However that said, I'm sure when they play live, the situation would be rectified. This is not Satch's best album, but it's ultimately pure Satch, so it by default makes it something worth getting your hands on.    Professor Satchafunkilus has entered the building

I am not a big contemporary book reader. YA or NA...but after reading a wonderful fantasy novel and going into a book hangover, I decided to pick up something a little different to give me time to soak in the wonderfulness of fantasy novels. And boy...was I surprised! I LOVED this book and Colleen Hoover's writing style was just what I was looking for.

Sydney and Ridge tore my heart apart, then helped me mend it, and then tore it apart once more before piecing it back together again. I thought the chemistry between Syd and Ridge was thoughtfully written and the progression in their relationship was just so well done. Without going into spoilers, I will say that this novel is relatable to a lot of people in their early to mid 20's. The topic of loving more than one person...or really emotionally cheating...is something that's really hard to deal with in a book. And to do it well...well that's just unheard of in NA.

Colleen Hoover has a great skill in writing physical attraction and she knows how to write a good male protagonist. Ridge was the right balance of manly and sensitive. The chapters where it was his POV sounded like him and not once did I get him and Syd's voices mixed up. I liked how Ridge and Syd didn't hide from their attractions and dealt with their issues face on without leaving a lot of room for miscommunication. I thought this was very important in this genre because oftentimes communication and having a couple of main characters hash out their feelings is so hard to do. It's like you are screaming into the book at those characters to just TALK ALREADY!

There's a couple of instances in this book that just had me tearing up at 4 am in the morning. For those that's read it, page 266 broke my heart!!! It totally caught me by surprise and the fact that Ridge told Syd that horrible story about him and his brother just made this scene even more heart wrenching. If Ms. Hoover's other books are anything close to this one (and from the ratings it seems like it is) then I'm on my road to becoming a fangirl. Actually, I have already ordered three more of her novels and they should be arriving tomorrow! 5 stars all the way!!!
